title: The Counsel and the Bank: Clark Clifford from Truman's White House to First American
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Fort Scott, the auditor's son
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On Christmas Day a son is born to Frank Clifford, who audits the books of the Missouri Pacific Railroad and travels the line to do it, and the boy is named Clark McAdams Clifford after his mother's brother. No birth address survives in any record reachable now; the pin marks the town and admits it. The family does not stay in Kansas. They settle in St. Louis, and the auditor's son grows up in a river city where the law is a trade a young man can enter without money behind him. He enters it in 1928 and stays fifteen years.
suggested_refs: Fort Scott, Kansas, and the Missouri Pacific Railroad line his father audited

stops.name: Washington University in St. Louis, the fraternity and the two degrees
stops.date_confidence: the initiation is attested to 1924 with no month or day, both defaulting to the first; the source gives no graduation year for either the BA or the LLB, and that omission is left standing as a gap.
stops.campa: On the campus above Forest Park he is initiated into the Beta Theta chapter of the Kappa Alpha Order, and out of the same university he takes a bachelor's degree and a bachelor of laws. The sources that record the fraternity year do not record the graduation years, so the file leaves them empty rather than guessing. He is a large, deliberate young man with a voice people remember before they remember what was said with it. It serves him in Truman's White House and, sixty-seven years on, in a Senate hearing room where it does not serve him.
suggested_refs: Brookings Hall and the Beta Theta chapter house, Washington University in St. Louis

stops.name: Downtown St. Louis, fifteen years at the bar
stops.date_confidence: the practice runs 1928 to 1943; the pin takes the opening year with month and day defaulted, and the firm's name and street address are a gap.
stops.campa: For fifteen years he tries cases in St. Louis, building the reputation of a trial lawyer whose gift is not thunder but the appearance of complete reasonableness. The firm's name and the number on its door are a gap; the pin is downtown, where the courts are. He is thirty-six when the war reaches him and takes him out of this practice, and he never comes back to it. The rooms he argues in after this one are in Washington, where the arguing is done to the men who appoint judges rather than to judges.
suggested_refs: The St. Louis trial bar of the 1930s, in which Clifford practiced for fifteen years

stops.name: St. Louis, marriage to Margery Kimball
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested; the ceremony's venue within the city is not given in any reachable source, so the pin is the city center.
stops.campa: He marries Margery Pepperell Kimball, called Marny. The marriage lasts sixty-seven years, which is longer than the career and longer than the money. Three daughters follow: Margery, called Gery, then Joyce Clifford Burland, then Randall Clifford Wight. The church or house of the ceremony is not named in anything reachable, so the pin is the city and nothing narrower. Sixty years on, when the New York assets are frozen and the federal indictment comes down, she has been married to him for sixty years and has seven left to go.
suggested_refs: The Clifford and Kimball families of St. Louis, joined 3 October 1931

stops.name: The White House, assistant naval aide to Truman
stops.date_confidence: the assignment is attested to 1945 with no month or day, both defaulting to the first; every naval posting between his 1944 commission and this door is a gap in the reachable record.
stops.campa: A naval officer in his late thirties arrives at the White House as assistant naval aide, and the arrival is the whole of what the record preserves about his war. Where he trained, which ship or district held him between commission and this door, no reachable source says. He is promoted to naval aide and reaches the rank of Captain. In October Robert Oppenheimer crosses this same threshold to tell Truman he has blood on his hands and is shown out; Clifford is inside the house that season in a junior uniform, and no source places him in the room.
suggested_refs: The naval aide's office in the wartime White House, 1945
sources: robert_oppenheimer.journey.json, for the October 1945 White House stop

stops.name: The White House, Special Counsel to the President
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the sources differ on the title, one giving White House Counsel and another Special Counsel to the President, and the difference is recorded in the report rather than resolved.
stops.campa: He takes off the uniform and stays. As Special Counsel he becomes the aide Truman reaches for first, drafting the language in which the administration says what it has decided to do. The title is not stable across sources: one calls the office White House Counsel, another Special Counsel to the President, and the file keeps the second because it is what the administration itself said. For four years the memoranda that shape containment, the armed services, and a reelection nobody expects him to win cross this desk.
suggested_refs: The office of the Special Counsel to the President under Truman, 1946-1950

stops.name: The White House, the Clifford-Elsey Report
stops.date_confidence: the source dates the report to 1946 with no month or day; the day defaults to the first and the month is placed after his appointment as Special Counsel in February so that the stop keeps travel order, which is a file convention and not a claim from any source.
stops.campa: With George Elsey he writes a top secret report for Truman cataloguing Soviet violations of the wartime agreements, a document that arrives in the same season as Kennan's argument from Moscow and pushes the same direction. The report is not published; its case becomes policy anyway. The sources give the year and no month, so the date here defaults. Clifford is thirty-nine, months out of the Navy, and the argument he has just co-signed is the one the government keeps for forty years.
suggested_refs: The Clifford-Elsey Report of 1946, delivered to Truman in secret

stops.name: Capitol Hill, the National Security Act
stops.date_confidence: the legislative work spans 1947 to 1949; the pin takes the first year with month and day defaulted, and no source itemizes Clifford's presence in the building on a named day.
stops.campa: The legislative campaign that produces the National Security Act of 1947 runs through this building, and Clifford works it from the other end of Pennsylvania Avenue: a Department of Defense, a National Security Council, a Central Intelligence Agency, all written into being in one statute and amended two years later. The pin marks the Capitol because that is where the law is made, not because any source puts him in a named room on a named day. He will run one of those creations twenty-one years from now.
suggested_refs: The National Security Act of 1947 and its 1949 amendments

stops.name: The White House, the campaign memorandum
stops.date_confidence: the sources credit Clifford with the 1948 strategy without dating the memorandum itself; month and day default to the first.
stops.campa: A memorandum lays out how a president nobody expects to win can win: hold labor, hold the West, run against the Congress rather than against Dewey, and get the man out of Washington and onto a train. The strategy is Clifford's in the form history keeps it, and Truman executes it to the letter. The sources date the approach to the campaign year without pinning the paper's own day. Truman wins in November, and Clifford, at forty-one, is the man credited in every account written afterward.
suggested_refs: The 1948 'Clifford Memo' and the whistle-stop strategy built on it

stops.name: The Oval Office, the recognition of Israel
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Against Secretary of State George Marshall, the most respected man in the government, Clifford argues in the Oval Office for immediate recognition of the state declaring itself that afternoon. David Niles argues beside him. Truman recognizes Israel the same day it declares independence. What Marshall said afterward goes unrecorded in the sources that survive. The counsel's judgment has outweighed the Secretary of State's. Nineteen years on, Clifford will be investigating that same state's attack on an American ship.
suggested_refs: The Oval Office meeting of 12-14 May 1948 on recognition of Israel

stops.name: Philadelphia, Convention Hall
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the convention month and venue are documented and Clifford's authorship of the campaign strategy is attested, but no source places him personally in the hall; the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: The Democratic convention nominates Truman for a race the newspapers have already awarded to Dewey, and sends him into a campaign built on Clifford's plan. Whether Clifford is himself in the hall is not attested; this pin is a reconstruction from the venue and his authorship, and it is carried as one. The plan is his, and it works in November against every prediction printed that summer. What he sells in Washington for the next four decades is the memory of that November.
suggested_refs: The 1948 Democratic National Convention at Philadelphia Convention Hall
sources: General historical record of the 1948 Democratic National Convention

segments.name: The Superlawyer and the Intelligence Board

stops.name: Lafayette Square, the office that overlooked the White House
stops.date_confidence: he leaves the White House on 31 January 1950 and the pin takes the following day; the office's street address is a gap and the coordinate approximates the vicinity his own description names.
stops.campa: The day after the counsel's office closes behind him he opens a law practice whose windows, in his own description, overlook the White House. The address itself is a gap; the pin approximates the square the phrase describes. He does not lobby in the crude sense and does not need to. Corporations and presidents pay him for the same commodity, which is to be told what Washington will do and who must be spoken to first. In this decade the word superlawyer is coined in this town, and it is coined for men doing what he is doing.
suggested_refs: Clifford's Washington law office near Lafayette Square, opened 1950

stops.name: Washington, the Kennedy transition
stops.date_confidence: the transition work follows the November 1960 election; the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: John F. Kennedy, whose lawyer he already is, hands him the transition into the new administration, and Clifford writes the memorandum that tells an incoming president how the government he has just won actually works. He takes no office in it. He has learned the arithmetic: a man inside the building has one client and a fixed salary, and a man across the street has all of them. Kennedy will give him an intelligence board within months, a seat that keeps him close to the government without putting him inside it. That arrangement holds until 1968.
suggested_refs: Clifford's 1960 transition memorandum for the incoming Kennedy administration

stops.name: The Eisenhower Executive Office Building, appointed to the intelligence board
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1961; the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: Kennedy appoints him to the President's Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board, the standing body that reviews the intelligence community from outside it, in the weeks after the Bay of Pigs has demonstrated what happens when nobody does. Clifford's part in that post-mortem is mentioned in the sources with no date attached to it at all, so it gets a paragraph in the report and no pin here. The board meets in the old State, War and Navy building beside the White House, close enough that a member can reach the president without leaving the grounds.
suggested_refs: The President's Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board, reconstituted after the Bay of Pigs

stops.name: The Eisenhower Executive Office Building, the chair of the board
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, as is the end of the tenure on 29 February 1968.
stops.campa: He succeeds James Killian as chairman and holds the chair four years and ten months, through the killing of the president who appointed him and into the presidency of the man who will send him to the Pentagon. He leaves it on the twenty-ninth of February 1968, the day before he takes over Defense. The board is renamed the President's Intelligence Advisory Board forty years later under a different administration; the research pool's first draft moved that renaming back into Clifford's tenure, and the correction is recorded in the report.
suggested_refs: The PFIAB chairmanship, 23 April 1963 to 29 February 1968

stops.name: Washington, the USS Liberty investigation
stops.date_confidence: the source gives the year of the investigation only; the pin takes June, the month of the attack, with the day defaulted.
stops.campa: An Israeli air and torpedo attack on a United States intelligence ship in the eastern Mediterranean kills American sailors, and the official investigation runs through Clifford's board. He calls it a flagrant act of gross negligence and presses Johnson to hold Israel accountable. Nineteen years earlier he stood in the Oval Office and argued for the recognition of that state against the Secretary of State who opposed it. The sources give the year of the inquiry and not its month; the pin takes June, when the ship was hit.
suggested_refs: The PFIAB inquiry into the 8 June 1967 attack on USS Liberty

stops.name: Saigon, Independence Palace
stops.date_confidence: the trip is attested to July 1967; the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: He flies to South Vietnam with General Maxwell Taylor on a mission to consult the allied governments and ask them for more, the errand the administration calls more flags. In Saigon he sees the war as it is described to him and the war as it is fought, and the distance between the two is the start of a change he does not announce. He comes home still saying in public what the administration says in public. Eight months later he is running the department that fights the war.
suggested_refs: The Clifford-Taylor mission to Saigon, July 1967
sources: FRUS 1964-1968, Vol. V, cited at second hand

stops.name: Canberra, Old Parliament House
stops.date_confidence: the visit is documented in the published diplomatic record; the pool gives no exact day, which defaults to the first.
stops.campa: At the old Parliament House on the hill, Clifford and Taylor spend a full day with the Australian government and talk privately with Prime Minister Harold Holt about raising the Australian contingent in Vietnam from six thousand five hundred toward nine thousand. In each capital of this circuit the two men ask the same question and count the same arithmetic. The research pool first pinned this meeting at the Parliament House opened in 1988, a building that does not exist in 1967, and the file uses the seat of government that did.
suggested_refs: Old Parliament House, Canberra, seat of the Australian government in 1967
sources: FRUS 1964-1968, Vol. V, Doc. 270, cited at second hand

stops.name: Wellington, the Parliament Buildings
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the mission's known circuit; no source reachable for this file places Clifford in these buildings on a named day, and month and day are both approximate.
stops.campa: The mission calls on the New Zealand government in the capital at the harbour's head, seeking further support for the allied effort in Vietnam. No surviving document places Clifford inside these buildings on a named day; the stop is carried as a reconstruction from the mission's circuit and tagged as one. What the smaller allies can send is small, and the men doing the asking know the size of it before they ask. The flags are the point, and both sides of the table know it before anyone sits down.
suggested_refs: The New Zealand Parliament Buildings, Wellington
sources: General historical record of the Clifford-Taylor 'more flags' mission

stops.name: Bangkok, Government House
stops.date_confidence: two lengthy meetings are documented in the published diplomatic record without a day given here; month and day are approximate.
stops.campa: At Government House he and Taylor meet the Thai prime minister and cabinet twice at length. The Thais agree that more Thai troops are needed and explain the difficulty in the plainest terms: they have men, and not enough officers to lead them. The research pool's first pass tagged this stop a reconstruction and set the pin some three quarters of a kilometre east of the building; the verifier found the meetings in the published diplomatic record and moved the coordinate onto Government House itself.
suggested_refs: Government House, Bangkok, and the Thai cabinet meetings of the 1967 mission
sources: FRUS 1964-1968, Vol. V, Doc. 270, cited at second hand

stops.name: Seoul, the presidential residence
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the mission's known circuit; no source reachable for this file names the building or the day, and month and day are both approximate.
stops.campa: The last call of the circuit is on the South Korean leadership, whose divisions are already in Vietnam in greater strength than any other ally's. Clifford asks for their continuation and their increase. As with Wellington and Manila, no reachable source puts him in a named building on a named day, and the stop is a reconstruction from the mission's route. He returns to Washington having asked six governments for soldiers, and having added up what six governments can spare.
suggested_refs: The South Korean presidential residence, Seoul, 1967
sources: General historical record of the Clifford-Taylor 'more flags' mission

stops.name: The Pentagon, sworn in
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the appointment itself is attested to 19 January 1968.
stops.campa: Johnson names him on the nineteenth of January and he is sworn in on the first of March as the ninth Secretary of Defense, succeeding Robert McNamara, who has been broken by the war he built. Clifford arrives with the reputation of a hawk and the appointment is read that way across the city. The Tet offensive is five weeks old and the military wants two hundred and six thousand more men. The new secretary begins by asking the question the building has not been made to answer in writing: what is the plan, and when does it end.
suggested_refs: The office of the Secretary of Defense, the Pentagon, March 1968

stops.name: The White House, the Wise Men reconvene
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25-26 March 1968; the pin takes the first of the two days.
stops.campa: Clifford has the Senior Advisory Group on Vietnam re-briefed and re-summoned: Acheson, Bohlen, Harriman, Kennan, Lovett, McCloy, Omar Bradley, the men Johnson calls the Wise Men and has trusted to tell him the war is winnable. Over two days they hear the briefers Clifford has arranged for them, and most of them come out saying it is not. The research pool's first pass recorded these meetings as undated and therefore unpinnable; the dates are in the record, and the verifier's correction restores them.
suggested_refs: The Senior Advisory Group on Vietnam, reconvened 25-26 March 1968
sources: General historical record of the Senior Advisory Group on Vietnam

stops.name: The Cabinet Room, the bombing halt above the twentieth parallel
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the last night of March, Johnson halts the bombing above the twentieth parallel, refuses Westmoreland the two hundred and six thousand men, and tells the country he will neither seek nor accept another term. Clifford's counsel is inside all three decisions. Eight weeks earlier he took office as the hawk brought in to steady a hawkish department. The men who appointed him for one purpose watch him accomplish the reverse of it, and the president who is finished says nothing to him about that afterward that any source records.
suggested_refs: Johnson's address of 31 March 1968 announcing the partial bombing halt

stops.name: Washington, the complete cessation of the bombing
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the last week of October the secretary supports what he could not have said aloud in February: the complete cessation of the bombing of North Vietnam. Johnson orders it. The election is days away and the negotiations in Paris are the thing being bought. In March he arrived asking for the plan. In October he has concluded there is not one. He has changed his mind inside the government, in eight months, without once resigning from it, and he keeps the office until January.
suggested_refs: The complete halt of the bombing of North Vietnam, 31 October 1968

stops.name: The Pentagon, the term ends and the medal
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Presidential Medal of Freedom with Distinction is awarded the same day.
stops.campa: His term closes with the administration that gave it to him, and on the same day Johnson hangs the Presidential Medal of Freedom with Distinction around his neck. He has been Secretary of Defense for ten months and twenty days. The war goes on for another six years without him. More than a decade later, in a recorded interview, he puts his conclusion in the plainest form he ever gives it, and the wording of that interview has not been checked against its own original transcript.
stops.quote: I found out that we couldn't win the war with the limitations that we had, which I thought were correct limitations.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Clark Clifford, WGBH Media Library and Archives Vietnam oral history, 1981; the transcript was not fetched and the wording is unverified, so the quotation is carried as reconstruction.
suggested_refs: The Presidential Medal of Freedom with Distinction, awarded 20 January 1969
sources: WGBH Media Library and Archives, Vietnam interview (1981), unverified

segments.name: The Elder Statesman and the Banker

stops.name: Washington, the first meeting with Agha Hasan Abedi
stops.date_confidence: Clifford's own Senate testimony places the meeting in December 1977; the Kerry-Brown report dates the introduction to 1978 and credits Bert Lance with making it, and the file keeps both rather than choosing. The day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: A Pakistani banker named Agha Hasan Abedi calls on him in the office that overlooks the White House, and they talk about a bank that means to bring banking to the Third World. Clifford will describe the meeting to a Senate subcommittee fourteen years later as brief and social. The Senate's own report dates the introduction to the following year and credits Bert Lance, Carter's budget director, with making it. Both dates are attested against their own sources; the file records both and adjudicates neither.
stops.quote: One of the main subjects we discussed in that brief social meeting was the aid that he had for his bank, of providing the Third World with banking services which they had not ever had before ... I found him to be pleasant and a man of importance.
stops.quote_source: Clark Clifford, Senate Subcommittee testimony describing his December 1977 meeting with Agha Hasan Abedi, in 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13
suggested_refs: Agha Hasan Abedi, founder of BCCI, queued in the atlas without a journey file of his own
sources: 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13
Wikipedia, 'Bank of Credit and Commerce International'

stops.name: New Delhi, special emissary for Carter
stops.date_confidence: the source gives the year only; month and day default to the first, and the venue within New Delhi is a gap, so the pin marks the seat of the Indian government.
stops.campa: Carter sends him to India as special presidential emissary, the fourth president to use him and the last. The sources name the country and not the room, so the pin marks the seat of the Indian government. He is seventy-three, and the phrase that travels with him now is adviser to presidents, a phrase whose number changes between sources: four where the count runs Truman, Kennedy, Johnson, Carter, and five in the bank documents that need him to be larger. The file names the presidents and avoids the number.
suggested_refs: Clifford's 1980 mission to India as special presidential emissary

stops.name: Washington, the hostage crisis and the threat of war
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the source reports the threat without naming a meeting, a room, or a date beyond the year; month and day default to the first and the pin approximates the State Department vicinity.
stops.campa: Americans are held in Tehran, and Clifford works the crisis from Washington, reported to have threatened Ayatollah Khomeini's government with war over its refusal to move. The report is carried as a reconstruction; no reachable source names the meeting or the room. Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi, whose throne that revolution ended, had come to Truman for arms in November 1949, in a White House where Clifford was Special Counsel. The file records the adjacency and claims nothing further from it.
suggested_refs: The Iran hostage negotiations of 1980 and Clifford's part in them

stops.name: The Federal Reserve, the hearing of April 1981
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in the Senate report's account of the hearing.
stops.campa: At a public hearing of the Federal Reserve, Clifford is asked directly what role the Bank of Credit and Commerce International will play in the affairs of the American bank its clients propose to buy. He answers that there is none. He also gives the regulators his reading of their conditions: that BCCI will acquire no stock at the tender offer, will not finance the purchase of stock, and will hold no control over the operation. Nine years later an audit finds the bank holding some sixty percent of the shares.
stops.quote: None. There is no function of any kind on the part of BCCI ... I know of no present relationship. I know of no planned future relationship that exists.
stops.quote_source: Clark Clifford, testimony at a public Federal Reserve hearing, 23 April 1981, in 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13
suggested_refs: The Federal Reserve hearing of 23 April 1981 on the Financial General Bankshares acquisition
sources: 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13

stops.name: Washington, the chairmanship of First American Bankshares
stops.date_confidence: the acquisition and chairmanship are attested to 1982 without month or day, both defaulting to the first; the headquarters address is a gap and the pin approximates downtown Washington.
stops.campa: Middle Eastern investors acting secretly as nominees for BCCI complete the purchase of Financial General Bankshares, rename it First American Bankshares, and Clifford takes the chairmanship because his name is the thing that quiets the regulators. Stuart Symington, once a senator, sits on the board with him. He is seventy-five and tells Congress it is a job he does with his own hands, having made a fundamental agreement with the shareholders, before accepting, that the authority would be his alone.
stops.quote: This was a hands-on occupation. I took it as my first obligation.
stops.quote_source: Clark Clifford, House Banking Committee testimony, in 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13
suggested_refs: First American Bankshares, Washington, chaired by Clifford 1982-1991
sources: Wikipedia, 'Bank of Credit and Commerce International'
'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13

stops.name: Calle 50, Panama City, the branch and its accounts
stops.date_confidence: the pin and its date are inherited byte-identical from the Noriega file, where the year is the earliest assigned to the Panama branch relationship and month and day are defaults; Clifford is not placed at this address by any source.
stops.campa: In the Panamanian banking district the same institution keeps the accounts of Manuel Noriega, and through them investigators later trace drug proceeds and covert payments moving in the same pipes, distinguishable only by paperwork. Clifford is not placed at this address by any source; what he shares with it is the letterhead and the chain of ownership above it. Asked in Washington how BCCI's officers stand to First American's owners, he answers that they are the representatives of the investors, which is the arrangement upside down.
stops.quote: We treat Mr. Abedi, we treat Mr. Naqvi, as the representatives of our investors.
stops.quote_source: Clark Clifford, Senate Subcommittee testimony, in 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13
suggested_refs: The BCCI Panama branch records entered in evidence in US v. Noriega
sources: 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13
Wikipedia, 'Bank of Credit and Commerce International'

stops.name: Washington, the shares bought with the bank's money
stops.date_confidence: the Senate report dates the CCAH stock purchases to 1986 without a day given here; month and day default to the first.
stops.campa: Clifford and his partner Robert Altman buy stock in the holding company of the bank Clifford chairs, using loans arranged by BCCI and secured by nothing but the shares themselves. He tells the Senate they had got over the hump and the time had come to participate in the results of a determined effort proving so successful. The profit he later acknowledges on bank stock bought with an unsecured BCCI loan is about six million dollars. He is seventy-nine and has never had to explain where money came from.
stops.quote: I wanted to own some stock in my own company.
stops.quote_source: Clark Clifford, Senate testimony on the 1986 CCAH stock purchases, in 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13
suggested_refs: The 1986 CCAH share purchases financed by BCCI-arranged loans
sources: 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13

stops.name: Leadenhall Street, the head office
stops.date_confidence: the pin and its date are inherited byte-identical from the Noriega file, where the London head office oversees the network throughout the 1980s and the year is arbitrary within that span; Clifford is not placed at this address by any source.
stops.campa: The principal London office runs the correspondent network through which money from Panama reaches everywhere else, and Abedi runs it from here. In 1990 a Price Waterhouse audit finds that BCCI secretly owns roughly sixty percent of First American, having seized the shares its own borrowers pledged as collateral; in 1991 regulators close the bank across seventy countries. Mark Lombardi will draw this network as arcs and nodes with Abedi and Clifford and North and Casey inside it. Manuel Noriega is one node, and Saddam Hussein's palace money is said to have crossed the same channels.
suggested_refs: BCCI's principal London office, Leadenhall Street; Mark Lombardi's BCCI-ICIC-FAB drawings
sources: US Senate Kerry Committee report on BCCI, 1992
Wikipedia, 'Bank of Credit and Commerce International'

stops.name: Capitol Hill, the subcommittee testimony
stops.date_confidence: the sources date the Kerry-Brown subcommittee testimony to 1991 without month or day, both defaulting to the first, so the stop's position inside the year is not fixed.
stops.campa: Before the subcommittee of Kerry and Brown he gives the defense he never changes: that he ran the bank honestly, that nothing in nine years looked wrong to him, and that if BCCI owned it behind his back then he was deceived. He adds that no law was violated and no impropriety committed. A former BCCI officer tells the same committee it is almost impossible to believe. The sources give the year without a month, so the position of this stop inside 1991 is not fixed and the file says so rather than inventing a day.
stops.quote: In all these years, we didn't encounter a single suspicious circumstance. ... Were we deceived? Apparently, we were deceived.
stops.quote_source: Clark Clifford, testimony before the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee on Terrorism, Narcotics and International Operations, in 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13
suggested_refs: The Kerry-Brown subcommittee hearings on BCCI, 1991
sources: 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13

stops.name: Washington, Counsel to the President is published
stops.date_confidence: the memoir is attested to 1991 and the C-SPAN Booknotes appearance to July; the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: Counsel to the President, written with Richard Holbrooke, reaches the bookstores in the year everything else reaches the newspapers. It is the account of Truman's White House by the last man able to give it firsthand, and it is published into a season in which his name has started to mean a bank instead. He discusses it on C-SPAN in July, courteous and unhurried, the voice unchanged since 1946. Two records of the same man are now running at once in opposite directions, and the book is the one he controls.
suggested_refs: Clark Clifford with Richard Holbrooke, Counsel to the President: A Memoir (1991)

stops.name: Manhattan, the District Attorney's disclosure
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Robert Morgenthau announces that BCCI has secretly owned First American all along, and indicts the bank, Abedi, and Swaleh Naqvi. The disclosure ends the arrangement Clifford chaired for nine years and opens the two proceedings that fill the rest of his life, one in Manhattan and one federal. He answers the way a lawyer of eighty-four answers, in the flattest language available to him, and the denial goes into a record that has already stopped turning on his word alone.
stops.quote: We have not violated any law. We have not been guilty of any impropriety.
stops.quote_source: Clark Clifford, Senate Subcommittee testimony, in 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13
suggested_refs: Morgenthau's 29 July 1991 indictment of BCCI, Abedi, and Naqvi
sources: Wikipedia, 'Bank of Credit and Commerce International'

stops.name: Washington, the resignation from First American
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the wire coverage of the resignations, which dates the quoted remark itself to April 1991.
stops.campa: Clifford and Altman resign from First American, the first American corporate casualties the wire services count in the collapse of BCCI. To a reporter that April he had already given the sentence that outlives everything else he said in seventy years of public life, a sentence in which both alternatives are ruinous and only one of them is criminal. The research pool first hung the line on his Senate testimony; the wire copy of this August day dates it to April and to a reporter, and the file follows the wire.
stops.quote: I have a choice of either seeming stupid or venal.
stops.quote_source: Clark Clifford to a reporter, April 1991, as quoted in UPI Archives, 'BCCI scandal claims first U.S. corporate victims,' 14 August 1991, and in the Deseret News of the same day
suggested_refs: UPI wire coverage of the Clifford and Altman resignations, 14 August 1991

stops.name: Washington, the indictment
stops.date_confidence: the indictment is attested to 1992 without month or day, both defaulting to the first; the pin is the federal courthouse as the venue of the federal proceedings.
stops.campa: A federal grand jury indicts Clifford and Altman for fraud, conspiracy, and taking bribes, and his investments in New York are frozen. He is eighty-five. The Kerry and Brown report, published the same year, finds the relationship with BCCI running back to 1978, four years before the chairmanship the two men describe as its beginning. A former regional officer of the bank has already told the committee what he makes of the claim that they did not know what they were chairing.
stops.quote: [I]t is very hard to believe, very, very hard to believe, almost impossible to believe ... that Clifford and Altman did not know [about BCCI's ownership of First American].
stops.quote_source: Abdur Sakhia, former BCCI regional officer, Senate Subcommittee testimony, in 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13
suggested_refs: The Kerry-Brown Senate report on BCCI, 1992
sources: 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13

stops.name: Manhattan, the trial of Robert Altman
stops.date_confidence: the trial and acquittal are attested to 1993 without month or day, both defaulting to the first.
stops.campa: Robert Altman stands trial in Manhattan and is acquitted, then signs a civil settlement with the Federal Reserve that bars him from banking for the rest of his life. He has denied the allegations totally and completely from the first hearing onward, beside the older man who brought him into the firm and then into the bank. Clifford is not in the courtroom with him. The case that would have tested the defense in front of a jury is the one his partner takes and wins.
stops.quote: The allegations that relate to misconduct on our part, I want the record to be clear, that we deny them totally and completely.
stops.quote_source: Robert Altman, Senate Subcommittee testimony, in 'The BCCI Affair,' U.S. Senate Report 102-140, Ch. 13
suggested_refs: The Manhattan trial and acquittal of Robert Altman, 1993

stops.name: Washington, the charges against Clifford end
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1993 without month or day, both defaulting to the first; the sources describe the ending two ways and the file does not choose between them.
stops.campa: The prosecutions end without a verdict on Clifford. The sources describe the ending in two forms, as charges dropped for his age and failing health and as a severance from the case on the ground that he is physically unable to stand trial, and the file carries both. He is eighty-six and is never tried. The research pool's first pass pinned this at the White House, an address with nothing to do with a prosecutor's decision; the pin here is the federal courthouse where the case was actually held.
suggested_refs: The E. Barrett Prettyman federal courthouse, Washington, venue of the federal BCCI proceedings
sources: Wikipedia, 'Bank of Credit and Commerce International'

stops.name: The Federal Reserve, the settlement
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1998 without month or day, both defaulting to the first.
stops.campa: Clifford and Altman settle with the Federal Reserve for five million dollars, and the last civil claim out of the BCCI affair closes. Altman has already accepted a lifetime bar from banking. Clifford is ninety-one and dies in the same year the papers are signed. Nothing in the settlement establishes what he knew or when he knew it. The question stays where he put it himself in April 1991, as a choice between two accounts of one man, and no court ever decides between them.
suggested_refs: The 1998 five-million-dollar Federal Reserve settlement with Clifford and Altman

stops.name: Bethesda, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; whether he died at home or in a hospital is not specified in any reachable source, so the pin is the town.
stops.campa: Clark Clifford dies at Bethesda, Maryland, at ninety-one. Whether in a hospital or at home no reachable source says, so the pin is the town and nothing narrower. The last time the public saw him he was a frail old man in a PBS documentary about Truman, a year earlier, speaking about the president whose counsel he had been half a century before. Tony Goldwyn had played him in one film by then, and Donald Sutherland will play him in another; both portraits stop before 1982.
suggested_refs: The 1997 PBS documentary Truman, Clifford's final public appearance

stops.name: Arlington National Cemetery, Section 7-A
stops.date_confidence: the burial is attested to 1998 with no day given, so the stop is pinned to the date of death; the funeral date itself is a gap and the plot number rests on tertiary crowd-maintained sources.
stops.campa: He is buried in Section 7-A, Grave 35, below the Memorial Amphitheater, among the officers and the government's dead. Arlington's own memorial page would not load, and the plot number comes from three crowd-maintained genealogies agreeing with one another, which is thinner ground than agreement usually looks. He served four presidents by the count that runs Truman, Kennedy, Johnson, and Carter, or five by the bank documents that needed him larger, and the two counts remain unreconciled.
